# Why Energy Stocks Are Down When They Should Be Up with Bob Brackett | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 60

First listed: 2026-05-18 | Evaluation cutoff: 2026-11-10

[Back to library](../README.md)

## Source versions

- [YouTube: Why Energy Stocks Are Down When They Should Be Up with Bob Brackett | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 60](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dFGIXqpyVzA) - 2026-05-18
- [Substack: Why Energy Stocks Are Down When They Should Be Up with Bob Brackett | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 60](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/why-energy-stocks-are-down-when-they) - 2026-05-18

Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

## Summary

Bob Brackett explains why near-term oil cash flows, forward curves and producer equities can diverge. He favors disciplined commodity exposure, dry-gas producers, Exxon, Diamondback and Cheniere while remaining tactically cautious on copper. Eisman adopts a cyclical entry-and-exit framework. Primary evidence supports severe supply disruption, regional gas congestion and strong producer cash generation, but several long-run scenarios remain unfinished and the storage-cost explanation has the wrong sign.

Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.

Since 1985, front versus six-month WTI was in contango about 42% of the time and backwardation 58%.

<a id="youtube-dFGIXqpyVzA-c011"></a>
### 011. Cheap-to-store commodities tend toward contango, whereas expensive-to-store oil and iron ore tend toward backwardation because of storage cost.

**Wrong** | Bob Brackett | analytical principle | major

[Source at 17:19-18:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dFGIXqpyVzA&t=1039s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

The storage-cost sign is reversed when other factors are held fixed. Carrying costs raise deferred prices; backwardation requires sufficiently strong convenience yield or other forces. Oil is not almost always backwardated.

Conditional reasoning: The carry relationship is F = S exp((r + u - y)T). Increasing storage cost u raises F relative to S, pushing toward contango, not backwardation.

Assessment test: Inspect the relevant original financial, operational or economic data and compare the claimed mechanism with competing explanations.

Further verification: Recheck the original data and subsequent realized outcomes.

- [Implications of WTI futures backwardation amid the supply crunch](https://www.cmegroup.com/insights/economic-research/2026/implications-of-wti-oil-futures-in-backwardation-amid-the-supply-crunch.html) (2026, April market observations): Explains that storage, insurance and financing costs contribute to contango; backwardation reflects convenience yield exceeding carrying costs. Since 1985, front versus six-month WTI was in contango about 42% of the time and backwardation 58%.

## Framework and tools

- Separate transit flows, shut-ins, inventory draws and net deficits.
- Value equities on cash flows and capital allocation, not spot commodities alone.
- Futures prices combine expectations, carry, convenience yield and risk premia.
- Distinguish resource estimates from commercially recoverable low-cost supply.
- Compare integrated, upstream, service and midstream risk separately.
- Strong demand growth can coexist with poor supplier returns when capacity overexpands.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Oil spot and forward curves.
- Commodity EBITDA sensitivity and net-debt bridge.
- Mining margins across cycles.
- Copper inventories and tariff scenarios.
- Gas basis, pipeline constraints and associated supply.
- FCF yields and LNG contracted capacity.
